sentences.pattern: The fact that + a post or image + has been widely shared does not mean that + it is reliable.
sentences.cn: 某项内容被广泛分享，并不意味着它具备某种可靠性。
sentences.example: The fact that a video has been widely shared does not mean that its caption is accurate.

sentences.pattern: Before accepting + an online claim, readers should establish who + created it + and what evidence supports it.
sentences.cn: 读者在接受某项说法前，应确认是谁发布了它以及依据何种证据。
sentences.example: Before accepting a health claim, readers should establish who published it and on what evidence.

sentences.pattern: What appears to be + independent advice + may in fact be + advertising, particularly when + payment or sponsorship is hidden.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Media-literacy lessons should use real material.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Students learn to evaluate media more effectively when they examine authentic posts, reports and images.
writingIdeas.argument: Definitions of bias are easy to memorise but difficult to apply when a polished video arrives through a trusted friend. In class, students can trace a current claim to its first publication, compare how several outlets frame it and explain which evidence changes their judgement. This process reveals that reliability is rarely determined by one visual clue. For example, a genuine photograph may still be paired with a false date. Guided analysis of real material therefore develops habits that transfer beyond an examination.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Platforms and users have different but connected responsibilities.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Improving the information environment requires both careful individual judgement and changes to platform design.
writingIdeas.argument: A user decides whether to repost a doubtful claim, but platforms determine which material receives rapid and repeated exposure. Systems designed mainly to reward engagement can amplify outrage before verification catches up. Platforms should label manipulated media, provide context from independent sources and reduce incentives for accounts that repeatedly distribute falsehoods. Individuals must still pause, cross-check and correct mistakes because no automated system understands every context. Responsibility should be shared in proportion to each party’s control over the spread of information.

speaking.question: Describe a time when you discovered that some information was misleading.
speaking.answer: I once saw a post claiming that a familiar food product had been recalled for safety reasons. The image looked official, and several friends had already forwarded it, so my first reaction was to believe it. Before passing it on, I searched the manufacturer’s website and found a genuine recall notice from three years earlier. Someone had removed the date and presented it as current news. I sent the updated link to the group and explained the mistake. What surprised me was that the photograph itself had not been edited; the missing context created the false impression. Since then, I have become much more careful about dates and original sources, especially when a post creates a sense of urgency.

speaking.question: Why do people share stories without checking whether they are true?
speaking.answer: Speed and emotion are probably the main reasons. People often encounter a story while doing something else, and sharing it takes only a second, whereas checking requires attention. A report that confirms an existing belief or creates anger also feels worth passing on immediately. In addition, users may trust the friend who sent it even though that friend did not create the content. I do not think most people intend to mislead others. Platforms could add useful friction, but individuals also need the habit of opening the article and checking its source before they amplify it.

reading.title: A Photograph Can Be Genuine and Still Mislead
paragraphs: Fact-checking advice often begins with image manipulation: look for an unnatural shadow, a repeated shape or a face produced by artificial intelligence. These clues matter, yet some of the most persuasive visual misinformation uses photographs that have not been altered at all. The deception lies instead in the relationship between an authentic image and the words, date or location attached to it.

During a flood, for example, an old photograph of a submerged road may circulate as evidence of current conditions in another country. A reverse-image search can reveal its earlier publication, but even that result requires interpretation. News organisations legitimately reuse archive photographs when they are clearly labelled, while social-media users may repost an image without knowing its origin. The central question is not simply whether the pixels are genuine but whether the new presentation supports the claim being made.

Captions have particular power because readers tend to treat them as instructions for seeing. In one experiment, participants who viewed the same crowd photograph with different political descriptions reported noticing different emotions and intentions. The image did not settle the disagreement; its ambiguity allowed each caption to organise attention. Where a photograph captures only a fraction of an event, material immediately outside the frame may also change its meaning—a quiet counter-protest, for instance, or the barrier that explains why people are running.

Verification teams combine several methods. They inspect landmarks, weather records and shadows; compare uploads to locate the earliest version; and contact photographers or local witnesses. None of these techniques is infallible in isolation. A timestamp may reflect the device setting rather than the moment of capture, and an early upload may still contain a false description. Confidence grows when independent clues converge.

Visual literacy therefore involves more than detecting sophisticated fakes. Readers should ask who supplied an image, what claim the caption adds and whether reliable sources place the scene in the same context. This approach is slower than reacting to a dramatic picture, but it prevents authenticity from becoming a shortcut to accuracy. A real photograph is evidence of something; careful verification establishes what.
